questions.stem: For counting sea service, how many hours equal one day?
questions.explanation: Eight hours of service equals one day of sea service. Twelve hours is the cap per calendar day and is worth 1.5 days.

questions.stem: How many credited days is a 12-hour watch worth?
questions.explanation: A 12-hour watch equals one and one-half days. One day is the value of an 8-hour day, and 2 days would require 16 hours, which is above the 12-hour cap.

questions.stem: A candidate has 72 credited days. How many months of qualifying service is that?
questions.explanation: Months are credited days divided by 30: 72 / 30 = 2.4. Dividing by 20 or 40 or using calendar months gives the wrong answers.

questions.stem: How many calendar days of 12-hour watches give 2 months of sea service?
questions.explanation: Two months is 60 credited days. Each 12-hour day is worth 1.5, so 60 / 1.5 = 40 days. Sixty is the number of 8-hour days, 30 gives only 45 credited days, and 45 gives 67.5.

questions.stem: A deckhand works one 15-hour day. How many credited days does it earn?
questions.explanation: Hours over 12 in a calendar day earn nothing extra, so the day counts as 12 hours = 1.5 days. 15 / 8 = 1.875 would ignore the cap.

questions.stem: A log shows 18 days at 8 hours, 20 days at 12 hours and 6 days at 4 hours (counting the short days in proportion to 8 hours). Does the candidate have 2 months?
options: No: 18 + 30 + 3 = 51 credited days, which is 1.7 months
Yes: 44 calendar days is more than 1.4 months and so enough
Yes: 18 + 20 + 6 = 44 days, which is over 1 month and so enough
No: 18 + 20 = 38 days, since short days do not count
questions.explanation: Credited days: 18 x 1 = 18; 20 x 1.5 = 30; 6 x 0.5 = 3. The total is 51, and 51 / 30 = 1.7 months, so about 9 credited days are missing. Counting calendar days instead of credited days gives a false pass. The 4-hour proportion is our straight-line reading of 'prorated'; the examiner confirms how short days are credited.

questions.stem: A candidate has 39 credited days. How many more 12-hour days are needed to reach 60 credited days?
questions.explanation: The shortfall is 60 - 39 = 21 credited days. At 1.5 per 12-hour day, 21 / 1.5 = 14. Twenty-one would be the answer only if every new day were an 8-hour day.

questions.stem: Sea service as a junior officer to the mate in charge of the deck watch is credited at what rate?
options: One and a half days for each day served
One day for each day served
Two thirds of a day for each day served
Half a day for each day served
questions.explanation: Section 117 credits that kind of service at two thirds of a day for each day actually served. It is lower, not higher, than normal service.

questions.stem: What must a sea service testimonial carry?
options: A copy of the vessel's registration
Nothing: the discharge book is enough
The required signatures and at least the information in Schedule 4 or 5
questions.explanation: Testimonials need the required signatures and at least the information set out in Schedule 4 or 5, and discharge books and certificates of discharge go with them. A self-signed note or a bare registration copy is not enough.

questions.stem: A candidate's service was on a vessel doing commercial work that was not carrying passengers or cargo, such as survey work. How is that service assessed?
options: It does not count at all
It counts in full under section 115
It counts at two thirds under section 117
questions.explanation: Section 116 sends service on other kinds of vessel and other commercial activities to Chapter 3 of TP 2293. Two thirds is the junior officer rate, which is a different situation.
